title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false-positive match in an automated licence-plate recognition system, occurring at the point where a camera alert was passed to a patrol deputy as grounds for a stop. The system compared a misread plate against a stolen-vehicle record and produced a hit on a vehicle that was not the stolen one. The failure sits at the handoff between machine output and human enforcement, because the alert was treated as sufficient cause to draw weapons rather than as a lead requiring confirmation.

Catching this would have required verification of the plate against the record before the stop, which the vendor itself states should happen. The reported contributing factor is a tinted cover on the plate, which the sheriff's office describes as illegal and which the facts indicate degraded the read. Whether the cover was in fact illegal, and whether the deputy had independent corroboration of a stolen vehicle before the stop, is not established by the reporting.

The account of the stop and its duration comes from a single outlet. The sheriff's characterisation of the deputy's conduct as reasonable is the agency's position, not an adjudicated finding, and no court or review body is reported to have ruled on the detention.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: A York County, South Carolina, man, Steven Melvin, 42, was detained at gunpoint for over five minutes after a Flock Safety license-plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office attributed the error to an illegal tinted plate cover and called the deputy’s actions reasonable. Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
